sources.citation: real-world (product class): the 120 V 100 W general-service incandescent lamp with a medium screw base (lamp makers' catalogues, typical published ratings, paraphrased, not one vendor's). Its hot resistance is V² / P = 14400 / 100 = 144 Ω and its rated current P / V = 0.8333 A.

game-design inside a read trend: Holladay (J. Opt. Soc. Am. 17, 1928, Table 5, read 2026-11-12 for the P3 lamp) gives gas-filled 50 W and 75 W lamps about 2685 K and 2735 K, rising with wattage; extrapolated linearly a 100 W lamp would run about 2785 K, which is not a reading. The P3 120 V lamp's 2700 K is kept, so every 120 V A19 bulb burns out at the same multiple of its rated voltage. With tungsten's resistivity (Jones and Langmuir, 1927) the cold resistance is 144 × 5.4849 / 81.095 = 9.74 Ω at 20 °C, 1/14.79 of the hot one.

Physics from H. A. Jones and I. Langmuir, General Electric Review 30 (1927): a filament's cold-to-hot resistance ratio is ρ(T_r)/ρ(T_a), 13.5 to 16.1 for rated temperatures of 2500 to 2900 K at a 293 K ambient; 14.79 at 2700 K. Source impedance and the wiring in series lower the current ratio, so the inrush is 10 to 15 times the settled current.

Physics estimate (the P3 D17 method applied to 100 W), recomputed in lighting-entries.spec.ts: a straight tungsten wire that radiates 95 W at 2700 K with a total emissivity of about 0.317 (Holladay 1928, Table 3) and has 144 Ω there (ρ = 81.095 µΩ·cm, Jones and Langmuir) is about 61 µm × 519 mm, 29.3 mg at 19.3 g/cm³; with tungsten's heat capacity at 2700 K (36.19 J/(mol·K), NIST-JANAF; 0.197 J/(g·K)) that is 5.76 mJ/K against a loss slope of 4 × 95 / 2700 + 5 / 2407 = 0.1428 W/K, τ ≈ 40.3 ms: a thicker wire stores more heat per watt radiated, τ scaling with the diameter. 40 ms is taken (the rounding is game-design); a coiled filament's self-shading would raise it (about 45 ms if 90 % of its surface radiates freely).

game-design inside published behaviour (P3 decision D17, paired with the time constant as the realism review recommended in P2): 5 % of the rated power is lost by conduction at the rated point, the rest radiated. The model's light fits the published L ∝ V^3.4 (Fink and Beaty) best near 5 %. A gas-filled lamp also loses heat to its gas, which the vacuum model doesn't carry; the one linear term stands in for end losses and gas both.

real-world: A19 is the A (standard household) bulb shape at a maximum diameter of 19 eighths of an inch, 2-3/8 in or 60.3 mm (the North American lamp-shape designation, ANSI C79.1 by number); drawn 60 mm across, rounded down, and 112 mm long overall, the 4.41 in of an A19 lamp datasheet read 2026-11-18. The base is the medium screw (E26).

game-design: the base's foot contact (a) at the bottom centre and its threaded shell (b) 12 mm up its side; neither takes a conductor, but a test lead's clip can grip either while the bulb is out of a socket.

real-world for the contacts, game-design for the place: a medium Edison screw base (E26, a 26 mm thread) screwed into a socket touches the socket's centre contact with its foot and the socket's screw shell with its threaded shell (the e26 mount type; lamp-base standards not cited by number). The bulb's origin sits 30 mm along and 30 mm across from the socket's axis, so its 60 mm body is centred on it (game-design anchor), and the fit takes the thread's 26 mm.

game-design (plan D3: an E26 base contact is game-design), an order-of-magnitude anchor, not a measurement: 2 mΩ for each of the foot and the shell, about the constriction resistance ρ / (2a) of one small contact spot of radius a = 15 µm in cartridge brass (about 28 % IACS, ρ ≈ 6.2 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m: 2.05 mΩ, Holm's single-spot formula), rounded down. A real shell touches at several thread points and the foot at one sprung tab; both are taken alike.
